newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power up slightly, Northwest colder.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power up slightly, Northwest colder.

text.p: Spot power prices in the western U.S. moved slightly higher amid expected cooler weather in the Pacific Northwest, trade sources said Thursday.
"It's a little bit cold here this morning," said a Portland, Ore., trader.
A northern California trader said power marketers needing to cover short positions and a decline in the number of utilities offering power also helped boost prices.
But after moving up as much as $4.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) in early trade, California-Oregon border (COB) quotes eased by $1.50 to $2.00 by mid-day, he added.
Bonneville Power Administration again refrained from offering surplus power for next-day delivery during peak hours.
Forecasts call for the Pacific Northwest to see slightly below-normal temperatures through next week, while the Southwest is expected to have slightly above-normal temperatures.
Friday firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) was quoted $16.00-16.50 per megawatt hour (MWh), up from $13.75-14.50 for Thursday.
Firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was slightly higher at $13.50-15.00, while off-peak was at $9.00-9.50.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity was also higher at $16.50-17.50, while off-peak was quoted $10.00-11.00 per MWh.
Next-day firm, peak prices at Four Corners were slightly up at $15.00-16.50, while off-peak was at $9.00-10.00.
